summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is criminal in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code covers any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural, and the sources disagree on the penalty it carries. Outright International records six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, about US$240 to US$720. The archived text of the 2020 code specifies two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. Human Dignity Trust gives a maximum of three years. A December 2024 press report cites Article 318 as carrying up to five years. The 1982 Penal Code that preceded the current one provided up to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.

Enforcement is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online, described as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 Penal Code. In June 2024 two women were detained after asking an imam to marry them; the marriage request was not proven in court, but the women stated they had previously had sexual activity together. On 12 December 2024 a Comoros court convicted them of homosexuality and sentenced them to five and six months respectively, releasing them immediately because the terms were shorter than the time already served. Human Dignity Trust called the case a human-rights violation.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report states that authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law that year. Police reported that they did not incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, and no such violence was reported in 2023. The same report lists widespread impunity among the country's major human-rights problems.

Transgender visitors and residents have no legal recognition to rely on. Legal gender markers cannot be changed, and no law prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code provides no protections for LGBTQ people, and the country has no non-discrimination law at all.

No LGBTIQ organisations operate in the country. Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF of 1986 prohibits associations founded on an unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose contrary to the law or public morals, which deters registration.

Relationship recognition offers nothing. The Family Code defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman, and no legal rights are recognised for same-sex couples, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no standing.

The government has repeatedly declined to decriminalise homosexuality when recommended by United Nations bodies.

Social conditions are documented as difficult: LGBTQ people face stigmatisation, and as of 2023 most did not disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity. Cultural discrimination affects access to education and employment, and some LGBTQ people are ostracised from homes, neighbourhoods and villages. No source in this inventory documents social treatment of transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
The penalty attached to the same conduct is reported four different ways across the sources, ranging from a six-month minimum to a five-year maximum, and the article number itself is given as 300 in three sources and 318 in one press report. A visitor cannot determine from these sources which figure a Comoran court would apply.

The 2023 enforcement picture and the 2022 and 2024 cases point in opposite directions: a year of no reported prosecutions sits between a leaked-video prosecution and the first conviction of a couple. Enforcement in this record is episodic rather than continuous, and the record does not establish a current rate.

The US State Department's 2010 report on Comoros contains limited material on LGBT issues; its substantive findings concern prison conditions, restrictions on movement, press and religion, and discrimination against women, which describe the general rights environment rather than trans-specific risk.

A 2023 Gallup figure found 26 percent of respondents saying the area they lived in would be a good place for LGBTQ+ people, ten percentage points above the previous year. The measure covers LGBTQ people generally, not transgender people, and is a national opinion indicator rather than a safety indicator.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot change the gender marker on their identity documents, and there is no legal route to recognition of a changed gender.

Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF blocks the formation of organisations whose stated purpose could be read as contrary to law or public morals, which is why no LGBTIQ group is registered or known to operate.

The 2012 Labor Code contains no protection for LGBTQ workers, and no general non-discrimination statute covers gender identity or sexual orientation.

Marriage under the Family Code is limited to a man and a woman, so same-sex couples hold no legal standing and no partner rights.

Most LGBTQ Comorans do not disclose their orientation or gender identity as of 2023, and ostracism from home, neighbourhood and village is documented alongside discrimination in schooling and employment.

The government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: which penalty provision and which article number a Comoran court would actually apply, given that the sources give four different ranges and two different article numbers for the same conduct.

Not sourced in this inventory: any rule on entry or visa screening of transgender travellers, any border or airport document-marker check, any treatment of binders, prosthetics or gender presentation during screening, and any rule on which gender a visitor's passport must show.

Not sourced: access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone availability, or any medical screening of arriving travellers.

Not sourced: any documented killing, assault or patterned violence against a transgender person in Comoros, with or without a date, so no trans-specific violence rate can be stated and none is implied here.

Not sourced: any data on how transgender people specifically are treated in society; the inventory's social figures cover LGBTQ people generally and stop at 2023.

Unresolved: whether the non-enforcement reported for 2023 reflects current practice, since the record contains prosecutions in 2022 and December 2024 but no enforcement data after December 2024.
